summary: Describes interfaces that the US National Security Agency profiles for servers that deliver certificates, certificate revocation lists, and symmetric keys to clients in National Security Systems. Such servers are called Secure Object Delivery Protocol servers. The audience is developers of client devices that get key management services from NSA-operated servers. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A special post office hands out keys and ID cards. This note explains how devices should ask it politely and correctly.

questions: what is secure object delivery protocol
how do clients get certificates from nsa servers
est and cmc protocols for key delivery
subtitle: NSA's specification for how secure servers deliver certificates, keys, and revocation lists to government devices.

tldr.problem: Government devices need secure ways to obtain public key certificates, symmetric keys, and certificate revocation information from authorized servers, but different implementations may not be compatible.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC specifies protocol interfaces (EST and CMC) and profiles for certificates, CRLs, and symmetric key delivery, with detailed requirements for trust anchors, certificate formats, and authentication.
tldr.outcome: Developers building government client devices know exactly how to request and validate keys and certificates from NSA-operated servers.

facts.label: Minimum Trust Anchors
facts.value: Two (one for PKI, one for keys)

today: RFC 9152 is an Informational RFC published in April 2022. It remains the current NSA specification for Secure Object Delivery Protocol servers and is not obsoleted.

sections.title: The SODP Server
sections.content:
The Secure Object Delivery Protocol (SODP) is a set of server interfaces for delivering secure objects (certificates, certificate revocation lists, and symmetric keys) to client devices in US National Security Systems. A SODP server uses two protocols: EST (Enrollment over Secure Transport) from RFC 7030 and its extensions from RFC 8295, and CMC (Certificate Management over CMS) from RFC 5274 and RFC 6402.

The profile applies to NSA-operated servers and is publicly available so that client device developers can build compatible implementations. Clients are not required to support all interfaces; they may choose which to implement based on their needs.
sections.eli5: The SODP server is like a special post office that hands out ID cards and secret keys. Clients are like devices that go to the post office and ask for them.

sections.title: Trust Anchors and Authorities
sections.content:
SODP uses a hierarchical trust model. A Source of Authority (SOA) is the top-level entity responsible for creating secure objects. An SOA can delegate authority by issuing certificates to Certification Authorities (CAs) and other entities. For symmetric keys, a Key Trust Anchor (KTA) may delegate to a Key Source Authority (KSA) that generates keys and a Key Distribution Authority (KDA) that distributes them.

Clients maintain an explicit trust anchor database of root certificates. Objects are secured using CMS (Cryptographic Message Syntax) content types, which provide digital signatures and encryption. All certificates and keys delivered by SODP servers must be validated back to an installed trust anchor.
sections.eli5: There is a big authority at the top that signs everything. Below that are helpers that create or hand out the cards and keys. Clients trust only the very top authority.

sections.title: EST and CMC Interfaces
sections.content:
EST (Enrollment over Secure Transport) is an HTTPS-based interface for certificate enrollment and key delivery. SODP servers provide EST endpoints including /cacerts (CA certificates), /simpleenroll (certificate enrollment), /crls (certificate revocation lists), and /symmetrickeys (symmetric key distribution). The /serverkeygen endpoint provides server-generated asymmetric keys in PKCS#12 format using AES-256 encryption.

CMC (Certificate Management over CMS) is an alternative protocol for certificate management that uses CMS-protected messages. Clients using CMC authenticate directly through message signatures rather than TLS client certificates, and can request full PKI operations.

Both protocols require TLS as configured in RFC 9151, with the notable requirement that only elliptic-curve algorithms are used (no RSA key transport). Clients reject HTTP redirects (3xx status codes) and validate all signatures against installed trust anchors.
sections.eli5: EST is a web post office where you ask for things over HTTPS. CMC is a more complex post office where messages are signed and sealed before asking. Both use the NSA's approved lock recipe.

sections.title: Certificate and CRL Profiles
sections.content:
SODP servers deliver three types of certificates: Trust Anchor certificates (self-signed root CAs), Certification Authority certificates (intermediate CAs), and End-Entity certificates (issued to clients and SOAs). All certificates use elliptic-curve algorithms only and follow the CNSA Suite Certificate Profile (RFC 8603).

Subject names are composed of standard attributes: country name, domain component, organization name, organizational unit name, common name, state or province name, distinguished name qualifier, and serial number. Trust anchors and non-self-signed CAs include specific extensions like the CRL Distribution Points extension, the Authority Key Identifier, and the Subject Key Identifier using the 64 low-order bits of the public key.

CRLs (Certificate Revocation Lists) are produced in two forms: complete base CRLs and partitioned base CRLs. All CRLs include the Authority Key Identifier and CRL Number extensions, and partitioned CRLs include the Issuing Distribution Point extension.
sections.eli5: The ID cards follow strict rules: what name you put on them, what information goes in them, and how to mark them as real. The revocation list is like a 'this card is fake' announcement.

sections.title: Client Authentication and Authorization
sections.content:
Clients authenticate to EST servers using Certificate TLS Authentication, where the client provides a certificate in response to a TLS CertificateRequest. For CMC, clients authenticate by signing protocol elements; all signatures are validated against installed trust anchors.

Clients must use an explicit trust anchor database with at least two trust anchors: one for PKI (certificates and CRLs) and one for symmetric keys. Clients check that the server's certificate includes the id-kp-cmcRA Extended Key Usage (EKU) value to verify the server is an authorized Registration Authority.

Clients that support the CMS Content Constraints extension validate that returned CMS content comes from an authorized SOA. Mutual authentication is required: both clients and servers reject any certificate that cannot be validated to an installed trust anchor.
sections.eli5: Before you talk to the post office, you show your ID card. The post office shows its ID card too. You both check that your cards are real and signed by the top authority. You trust each other only if both cards check out.

sections.title: Security Practices
sections.content:
SODP requires that symmetric key packages are encrypted and signed using CMS content types. The RFC specifies algorithms: AES-256 Key Wrap with Padding for key wrapping and content encryption (never AES-128). PKCS#12 (PFX) files for server-generated keys use HMAC-SHA-384 for the PBKDF2 key derivation function and AES-256 for encryption.

Clients must request certificate revocation status information via CRL distribution points or OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol). All certificate enrollments are restricted to devices that have an established prior relationship with the Registration Authority, verified out-of-band before EST or CMC enrollment begins.
sections.eli5: Secret keys are always wrapped up (encrypted and signed) before they are sent. Every ID card must be checked against a list of fake cards. Only devices that the post office already knows are allowed to ask for new cards.
